transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, um... well, to be honest, I came in because I just—I can’t shut my brain off anymore. It's like a motor that's just constantly running and overheating, you know? I'm an IT systems manager, and my days are already stressful enough managing different networks and teams, but lately... well, it’s not even just lately, it’s been building up for a while. 

It always starts with just one small concern. Like, for example, just the other day, I had a client who wasn't responding to a routine email about a system migration. Just a normal delay, right? People get busy, they step away from their desks. But my mind just grabs onto it, and within minutes—literally minutes—I’m completely convinced that they hate our work and I’m going to lose the entire contract. 

And then, because my brain won't just stop there, it keeps going. I start thinking about how if I lose the contract, my department's numbers will tank, and then I'll get let go. And if I lose my job, I'm going to fall behind on my divorce payments. My ex-wife is already on my case about everything, and if I miss a payment, the legal fallout is going to be an absolute disaster. And then I start spiraling into this really dark place where I'm convinced I'll be completely ruined, my reputation in the industry will be destroyed, and I'll never get back to a real leadership role again. 

It’s just exhausting. I sit there staring at my monitors, and I can't even focus on the actual work because I'm basically living out this entire catastrophic future in my head, all over a single unreturned email. And it just keeps happening, over and over, with almost everything I do. I just can't stop it.
Is this kind of worrying happening just with work-related things or is it also happening with other areas of your life?

Oh, no, it’s... I wish it were just work, to be honest with you. If it was just work, maybe I could just turn off my monitors and leave it at the office, but it bleeds into literally everything else. It’s like this chain reaction that I have absolutely no control over. 

My mind just keeps jumping from one disaster to the next without any breaks. I’ll be stressing about the contract work, right? And then, within seconds, my brain just completely shifts gears and I'm agonizing over my mortgage payments. I'll start running the math in my head, thinking about what happens if I miss a payment, if the bank forecloses, where I'm going to live, how I'm going to afford anything with the way the economy is right now. 

And then from the mortgage, it jumps right to my reputation, which is a whole other spiral. The tech circles around Bethesda, where I am, they're incredibly tight-knit, you know? Everyone talks, everyone goes to the same networking events. So I start obsessing over whether people in those Bethesda tech circles think I’m just... damaged goods now. Like, maybe they know about the messy divorce, or maybe they sense I'm slipping at work, and I just convince myself that I'm becoming this industry pariah and nobody will ever want to work with me again. 

I mean, it gets so bad that even the smallest things trigger a total meltdown. Like, I was waiting on a message from a recruiter recently—just putting some feelers out there because I was already panicking about getting fired—and the response was delayed. Just a normal delay, right? But my brain couldn't handle it. To me, a delayed email from a recruiter can feel like absolute, undeniable proof that my whole career is closing down. That it's over. That nobody wants to hire me, that I'm completely washed up at forty-seven, and I'll never work in IT management again. 

It just never stops jumping around. It goes from the contract, to the house, to what people think of me, to my entire future being ruined, all before lunch. And I just... I don't know how to break the cycle because every time I try to rationalize one worry, my brain just finds three more things in my personal life to completely panic about.
Do you feel like this constant worrying is significantly interfering with your daily life or relationships?

Yeah, it really is. I mean, it's... it's taking a toll on basically everything at this point. It’s not just the feeling of being stressed, it’s actually stopping me from doing things I need to do. At work, for instance, I’ve completely dropped the ball on some networking follow-ups. I mean, these are important contacts, people I really need to stay in touch with, especially with how worried I am about my job security. But I just sit there staring at the draft, and I start anticipating every single thing that could go wrong. Like, what if my tone is too desperate? What if they think I'm bothering them? What if they mention it to someone else and it makes me look weak? And before I know it, an hour has passed and I haven't sent the email. 

And it's not just networking, either. It's actual client deliverables. I’ve had to delay sending things out because I get so paralyzed by the "what ifs." I'll check a system report ten, fifteen times, convinced I missed something catastrophic, and then I miss the deadline anyway because I was too busy panicking to just hit send. It's incredibly frustrating because I know I'm good at my job—or I used to be—but this constant dread is just making me freeze up.

And then outside of work... well, it’s affecting that too. I used to play in a local soccer league on the weekends. Just a casual thing, you know, a way to blow off steam and hang out with some guys I've known for years. But I’ve completely pulled back from that. I haven't been in weeks. Honestly, I'm just so tense all the time, and I'm exhausted from the constant worrying, that I end up being really irritable. I snap at people over the smallest things. The last time I went, I got into this ridiculous argument with a friend over a bad call, and I just felt so embarrassed afterward. I don't want to be that guy, you know? The one who's always on edge and snapping at his friends. So I just stopped going. I isolate myself because I don't want people to see how much I'm struggling, but then being alone just gives me more time to sit and worry about how I'm pushing everyone away. It's just this horrible, vicious cycle.
Do you worry about being judged or evaluated by others in social situations?

Um... no, not exactly. I mean, I wouldn't say it's the social situation itself that makes me anxious, if that makes sense? Like, if I'm at a barbecue or a dinner or something, I'm not sitting there sweating about whether people think I'm holding my drink weird, or if I'm chewing too loud, or if I'm saying the wrong thing in a casual conversation. It's not like I have stage fright or anything like that. I mean, I manage teams of IT professionals, right? I have to run meetings all the time, present quarterly reports, and the actual act of standing up and speaking or interacting with people doesn't bother me at all. I've always been pretty comfortable working a room. 

It's more... well, like I was saying before about those Bethesda tech circles, it's not that I'm afraid of the *interacting* part. It's that my brain is constantly running these catastrophic scenarios in the background. So, if I go to a networking event, I'm not anxious because it's a social event where people are looking at me. I'm anxious because my brain is telling me, "These people know your department's numbers are slipping, and they know your life is a mess, and you're going to be blacklisted." It’s the career and financial consequences I’m terrified of, not the socializing itself. 

Or, you know, I could be at a neighborhood block party, completely unrelated to work, just talking to a neighbor about, I don't know, lawnmowers or property taxes or something. And I'm not worried they're judging my small talk. But while I'm standing there nodding and pretending to listen, my brain is just screaming at me that I forgot to double-check the server migration protocols before I left the office on Friday, and if there's a data breach over the weekend, I'm completely ruined and won't be able to pay my legal fees for the divorce. So my mind is a million miles away, panicking about my whole life collapsing. 

So I guess... no, I don't really worry about being evaluated socially in the moment. It's just that my brain never stops running through all the other disasters waiting to happen, no matter who I happen to be standing in front of.
Are there any specific objects, places, or situations that trigger your worrying or anxiety?

Um... no, not really. I mean, I wish it were that simple, honestly. If it was just, you know, a fear of dogs or elevators or something... I could just avoid those things, right? I'd just take the stairs for the rest of my life and be perfectly fine. But it’s not tied to anything specific like that. It’s not an object or a place. It’s just... everywhere. 

I could be sitting in my car in my own driveway—perfectly safe, engine off, just sitting there—and my mind is just racing a mile a minute because I'm thinking about a server migration that might fail over the weekend. Or I could be at the dentist getting my teeth cleaned, and instead of worrying about the drill like a normal person, I'm agonizing over the legal fees from the divorce and whether my lawyer is billing me for every single email. So it’s not the car, and it's not the dentist's office. The environment doesn't matter at all. 

The worry is just like this... this background radiation that’s always there, no matter where I go or what I'm looking at. It doesn't need a specific trigger to start up. It just generates itself, if that makes sense? I mean, I've actually tried to track it. Being an IT guy, I like data, I like finding the root cause of an issue, so I tried to see if there was a pattern. Like, does it happen more in the conference room? Does it happen more when I'm at home on the couch? But the data is just a flat line at maximum capacity all the time. There's no specific trigger, it's just my default state of being now. I wake up and the engine is already running hot, and it stays that way no matter what room I walk into or what object I'm holding. It's just exhausting.
Do you ever experience any physical symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or trembling when you're worrying?

Um... no, actually. Not really. I mean, I know that’s what people usually think of when you talk about worrying, right? You picture someone hyperventilating into a paper bag, or sweating through their shirt, or their hands are shaking so much they can't even hold a coffee cup. But for me, it’s not... it's not like this sudden, dramatic physical explosion where my heart is pounding out of my chest. I'm not sitting there checking my pulse or anything like that. 

It’s funny, because my ex-wife used to say I was like a duck on a pond—you know, completely still on the surface, but paddling like crazy underneath. And that's kind of exactly how this is. Physically, on the outside, I don't get the cold sweats, I don't tremble, my heart isn't racing. If you looked at me sitting in a meeting or staring at my laptop, you wouldn't see a guy who's physically freaking out. You'd just see a guy sitting very, very still. 

But internally, my brain is just... it's like a server processor maxed out at 100 percent utilization, just running all these catastrophic calculations over and over and over again. So the racing is entirely mental. It's my thoughts that are racing, not my heart. I just sit there, staring at a screen or a wall, completely paralyzed by all the "what ifs" I mentioned earlier. But as far as the physical stuff you're asking about—the sweating, the shaking, the palpitations—no, I haven't really experienced any of that. It's just this constant, exhausting mental loop that never shuts off, but my body itself isn't doing the trembling or sweating thing.
How long have you been experiencing this constant worrying?

Well, let's see... it's been a while now. I can actually pinpoint it pretty exactly, which I guess is the IT manager in me, right? I trace it back to when the floor really fell out from under me. It was about thirteen months ago. That's when I got let go from my last full-time position. And I mean, getting fired is stressful for anyone, obviously, but for me, it was like someone flipped a switch in my brain and broke off the handle so I couldn't turn it back off. 

At first, I thought, okay, it's just the shock of the job loss. You know, you lose your income, your routine, your sense of stability, and you panic. That's normal. I told myself it would pass once I got back on my feet. And I did hustle, I really did. I managed to land some contract work eventually—not exactly the Director-level stuff I was used to, but it was income, it kept the lights on while I was dealing with the divorce and everything else. 

But the thing is... the worry didn't stop when I got the contract work. If anything, it just mutated. Instead of worrying about not having a job, I started agonizing over whether the contract would be renewed, or if I'd make a mistake and they'd terminate the contract early, or if the IRS was going to audit my 1099 income. It was like my brain had gotten so used to running at that maximum capacity of panic that it just refused to spool down, even when the immediate crisis was technically resolved. 

So yeah, it's been thirteen months of this. Thirteen months of waking up every single day with that engine running hot, like I mentioned before. And it's exhausting, honestly. I keep waiting for the day I wake up and my brain is quiet, but it just hasn't happened since the day I packed up my desk over a year ago. It just never really let up.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain tasks or activities because of your worrying?

Yeah... yeah, I do. And it's really starting to mess things up for me, honestly. You know, you'd think that worrying so much would make you hyper-productive, right? Like you'd be on top of everything just to prevent bad things from happening. But it's actually the exact opposite. It's paralyzing. 

Take my contract work, for example. I'm doing these IT consulting gigs now, which means I really need to be hustling, right? I need to be networking, sending follow-up emails, maintaining relationships. But I'll sit down to draft an email to a potential client, or even just a follow-up to someone I met on LinkedIn, and I just... I freeze. My brain starts running all these scenarios. What if my tone is too desperate? What if I sound arrogant? What if they read it and think I'm completely unqualified because of that gap in my resume? What if they forward it to someone else and laugh at it? I'll spend three hours staring at a two-line email, rewriting it twenty times, and then I just close the draft and don't send it at all. So I've missed out on all these networking follow-ups that I desperately need to be doing. 

And it's not just the new business, it's the actual work, too. I've delayed client deliverables—which is a huge deal in my line of work, you do not miss deadlines—because I get so stuck anticipating every single thing that could possibly go wrong with a deployment or a system architecture plan. I'll test it, and then test it again, and then think of some obscure, one-in-a-million edge case where the system might fail, and I'll spend two days trying to mitigate a risk that doesn't even really exist. By the time I finally hand the work over, it's late, and I'm stressed, and the client is annoyed. 

And it bleeds into my personal life, too, what's left of it anyway. I used to play in this recreational soccer league on Thursday nights. Nothing serious, just a bunch of middle-aged guys trying not to pull a hamstring, right? Then maybe grab a beer after. But I've completely pulled back from that. I haven't been in months. I've stopped hanging out with my friends, too. Because... well, honestly, I'm just embarrassed. I'm embarrassed by how tense I am all the time. I'm irritable, I snap at people over nothing, I can't follow a conversation because I'm busy worrying about whether my ex-wife's lawyer is going to file another motion... and people notice. You can't hide that kind of tension. My friends would ask if I was okay, and I'd just get defensive. So it's easier just to avoid them. Avoid the soccer games, avoid the networking, avoid hitting "send" on the deliverables. It's like my world is just shrinking down to my laptop screen and my couch, and even then, I can't get anything done.
Do you worry about what others think of you when you're in social situations?

You know, it's funny you ask that, because I think people always assume that if you're a tense or worried person, you must be constantly stressing about people judging you. But... no. Not really. I mean, sure, in a professional context I worry about a client thinking my work is bad, but that's entirely tied to losing the contract, right? That's about the money and the survival of it all. But just general social situations? Like being at a barbecue or hanging out with the soccer guys? No. I'm not sitting there wondering if they think I'm cool or if I said the wrong thing or if my shirt looks stupid. 

It's not that kind of high school popularity worry. It's more like... I just don't have the processing power left to care. Like I said before with the server processor analogy—if my internal CPU is running at 100 percent capacity just dealing with the divorce and the job loss and the IRS, there's literally zero memory left to allocate to, you know, "Does Dave think my joke was funny?" I just... I don't care about Dave's opinion. 

What I care about is that while I'm standing there talking to Dave about his golf swing, I'm not working. And if I'm not working, I'm not billing hours, and if I'm not billing hours, my whole life is going to completely unravel. So the whole time I'm in a social situation, I'm not worried about the people around me, I'm just agonizing over the fact that I should be doing something else to fix my life, or I'm running through what my ex-wife's lawyer might be doing right at that exact moment. 

It's like... if your house is on fire, you don't really care if the neighbors think your pajamas are out of style while you're standing on the lawn, right? You're just focused on the fire. That's how my brain works right now. The house is always on fire. So yeah, I avoid people, and I isolate myself, but it's not because I'm worried about what they think of me. It's just that I can't handle the effort it takes to stand there and pretend the house isn't burning down. It takes so much energy to nod and smile and maintain a normal conversation when you're internally vibrating with stress about a million other things. So, no, the social judgment thing isn't really on my radar at all. I'm just too busy managing the constant, invisible crisis in my head to even factor in what someone else thinks of me.
Do you feel like your worrying is causing you a lot of emotional pain or distress?

Pain? I mean... I'm not really sure if I'd use the word "pain," exactly. When I think of emotional pain, I think of, you know, profound grief, or sitting around crying all day, and that's not really what this is. But distress? Yeah. Absolutely. A massive amount of distress. It's just... it's a very specific kind of misery, I guess. 

You know how it is when you're just constantly waiting for the other shoe to drop? It's like my brain is stuck in this endless loop of worst-case scenarios, and it just wears you down to the absolute bone. I'll sit there on my couch, and I'm physically safe, the doors are locked, I'm just looking at my laptop, but emotionally? I'm completely drained. It's this heavy, crushing weight. It makes me feel so incredibly isolated. Because, like I said, I've got the job stuff and the divorce, and instead of just dealing with those things one step at a time like a rational adult, I'm trapped in this relentless cycle of... just absolute dread about what's coming next. 

And that is incredibly distressing. It's like being locked in a server room where the critical failure alarms are blaring at maximum volume 24/7, but nobody else can hear them, and you can't find the mute button. You start to feel like you're losing your mind. I'll look out the window and see people walking their dogs, getting coffee, just living their lives, and I honestly just stare at them and think, "How are you doing that? How is your brain letting you just exist?" Realizing that I can't do that anymore—that I can't just be present and at peace for even five minutes—that's what really gets to me. It's exhausting, and it's lonely, and yeah, it's profoundly distressing. I just want it to stop, you know? I just want a break from my own head.
Do you often find it difficult to control your worry once it starts?

Oh, absolutely. That's... honestly, that's exactly why I finally made the appointment to come in here. I just can't shut my brain off anymore. It's impossible. Once a worry takes root, I have zero control over it. It's like a runaway script in a database, you know? An infinite loop that just keeps consuming more and more processing power until the whole system completely locks up. I can't hit the brakes.

It always starts with something so small, too, which is the most frustrating part. Just one little, everyday concern. Like, say I send an email to a client with a proposal or an update, and they don't respond right away. A normal person would probably just think, "Oh, they're in a meeting, they went to lunch, they'll get to it later." But my brain? No. My brain immediately jumps to the worst possible conclusion. Within minutes—literally minutes of not getting a reply—I'm sitting there staring at my screen, completely convinced that they're ignoring me because they hate the work I did. 

And then the dominoes just start falling, and they fall fast. If they hate the work, then I'm definitely going to lose the contract. If I lose that contract, the revenue stream dries up. If the revenue stream dries up, how am I going to make my divorce payments? My ex-wife's lawyer is already looking for any excuse to drag me back into mediation, so if I fall behind on those payments, I'm going to end up in court again, which costs money I don't have. And while I'm spiraling about the legal fees, my brain just pivots right into my career trajectory. I start thinking about how I used to be an actual IT manager. I had a team, a steady salary, a title. And now I'm just scraping by on these independent consulting gigs, and if I can't even hold onto this one client, I'm never going to get back to a real leadership role. I'll just be this washed-up, middle-aged guy who couldn't keep his career or his marriage together. 

So it goes from "the client hasn't emailed me back in an hour" to "my entire life is permanently ruined" in the span of maybe ten or fifteen minutes. And the craziest part is, a tiny, rational part of my brain knows exactly what's happening. I know I'm spiraling. But I just can't stop it. I can't reason with it or tell myself to calm down. The worry just takes the wheel and drives me right off a cliff, every single time.
Have you noticed any significant problems at work or in your personal relationships as a direct result of your worrying?

Yeah. Yeah, it’s... it’s bleeding into absolutely everything at this point. Both work and my personal life, which is just fantastic, right? Just exactly what I need right now. 

On the professional side, I mean, it’s actively hurting my business. I’ve completely dropped the ball on networking follow-ups. I’ll actually force myself to go to a local business mixer, hand out cards, meet some decent contacts, and then the next day when I'm supposed to reach out... I just can't. I sit there staring at a draft, and I get completely stuck anticipating every single thing that could possibly go wrong. What if I sound too desperate for work? What if they were just being polite and don’t actually want to hear from me? What if I actually get their project and completely mess it up? So I just... don't send the email. The opportunity just dies. 

And even worse than that, I’ve actually delayed client deliverables. Like, the work is done. It’s finished, sitting right there on my hard drive. But I won’t send the final files because I’m paralyzed. I'll go over the system architecture or the network maps again and again, terrified I missed some fatal flaw that’s going to ruin my reputation and get me sued. It’s infuriating because I know I need the money to survive, but the dread just completely overrides my logic. 

And then, you know, on the personal side... it’s just as much of a disaster. I used to have a pretty good group of guys I hung out with. We had this weekend soccer league. Nothing serious, just a bunch of middle-aged guys running around and then grabbing a beer afterward. But I’ve completely pulled back from all of it. I don’t go to the games anymore, I don't go to the pub, I barely even answer their texts to hang out. 

And it’s not because I don’t like them, it’s because... well, honestly, I’m just embarrassed. I’m embarrassed by what I’ve turned into. I am so tense all the time, just physically wound up like a coiled spring, and it makes me incredibly irritable. If I go out with them, I can’t just relax and have a good time. Someone makes a harmless joke, or the ref makes a bad call on the field, and I just snap. I have zero patience. I can feel myself ruining the mood, being the miserable guy who brings the whole group down because I can't take a joke or let something slide. So instead of inflicting myself on my friends and having them look at me like I'm crazy, I just stay home. I isolate. It’s just... it’s easier to cut myself off than to try and explain why I'm so tense and irritable all the time.
Are you having trouble sleeping due to your worrying?

Sleep? Oh, God, sleep is... it's practically a joke at this point. I mean, I try to do everything right, you know? I'll turn off my laptop, I'll try to wind down, but the absolute second my head hits the pillow, it’s like my brain just boots up into high gear. The quiet actually makes it worse. 

Most nights, I just lie there in the dark, completely wired, and my mind just starts chewing on everything. I’ll find myself replaying interview answers from weeks ago—because I've been trying to interview for some full-time roles to get out of this consulting mess—and I'll just lie there dissecting every single word I said, completely convinced I sounded like an idiot and ruined my chances. And while I'm doing this, I'm just watching the time slip away. I’ll roll over and check the clock, and it’s 2 a.m. Then I'll toss and turn, try to force my eyes shut, and I'm checking it again, and it’s 3 a.m. It’s just this agonizing countdown to morning, doing this mental math of "if I fall asleep right now, I can get four hours... if I fall asleep now, I can get three hours." 

And the really frustrating part, the part that just completely drains me, is that even on the rare nights where I supposedly get enough sleep—like if I actually manage to string together seven or eight hours of unconsciousness—it doesn't even matter. It doesn't feel like rest at all. I wake up the next morning feeling exactly like I did back when I was an IT manager and I’d spend the entire night on call for a massive system outage. You know that feeling? Where you're just running on pure adrenaline and dread, and your eyes are gritty, and your body actually aches from being so tense for hours on end? That is how I wake up every single day now. I wake up feeling like I’ve been fighting a server fire all night long. And then I have to drag myself out of bed and somehow pretend to be a functioning human being for the next sixteen hours, which just feeds right back into the anxiety about not performing well, because I'm so exhausted I can barely see straight. It's just a nightmare. I don't even know what a real night's sleep feels like anymore.
Are there any situations or activities that you avoid because they might trigger or worsen your worrying?

Avoid? I mean... no. Not exactly. Not in the sense that you're talking about, I don't think. It's not like... well, it's not like there's a specific button I can just choose not to press to keep the whole system from crashing, you know? 

I know I mentioned earlier that I stopped going to the pub with the guys, and that I'll put off sending those final client emails, but that’s... that's more because the anxiety has already made me a total wreck, not because those specific things *trigger* the worry. The worry is already running. It's always running. 

It's not like I can say, "Oh, if I just don't go to the grocery store, or if I don't drive on the highway, I won't have a spiral." Because I could be sitting on my living room couch, staring at a completely blank wall, doing absolutely nothing, and my brain will just invent a massive crisis out of thin air. It’s exactly like a background process on a computer that’s just permanently running, eating up 99 percent of your RAM, no matter what application you actually have open on the desktop. 

So, no, there aren't really specific situations or activities I avoid to try and stop the worry from starting, because honestly, it doesn't matter what I'm doing. I could be taking a shower, or trying to read a book, or just making a cup of coffee, and suddenly I'm agonizing over my tax returns from three years ago, or I'm terrified I forgot to renew a critical software license for a client, or I'm obsessing over some offhand comment my ex-wife made during the divorce proceedings. There’s no... there's no safe zone I can retreat to where it doesn't happen. The calls are coming from inside the house, so to speak. So trying to avoid things to stop the worry would basically mean avoiding existing altogether. And knowing my brain, I'd probably just find a way to stress out about that, too.
Do you think your worrying about what others might think of you is affecting your relationships or daily activities?

I mean... no. Not really. I know I said earlier that I didn't want my friends looking at me like I was crazy when I snap at them, but that’s... that's different. That's just me knowing I'm being a miserable jerk and not wanting to inflict that on them. It’s not like I’m sitting around agonizing over whether people like me, or if they think I’m smart or funny or whatever. 

It’s not a... it's not a social judgment thing. I really don't care what people think of my personality or my clothes or anything like that. My worries are always so much more... I guess, operational? Like, catastrophic failures. When I'm stuck in my head, I'm not worried that the guy at the coffee shop thought I was weird. I'm worried that I misconfigured a firewall for a client and their entire network is going to get breached, and I'm going to get sued, and I won't be able to pay my mortgage, and I'll end up completely ruined. 

So, if my relationships are falling apart—which, let's be honest, they absolutely are—it’s not because I'm scared of what my friends think of me. It’s just that I literally do not have the bandwidth to deal with other human beings. When your brain is running, you know, a hundred different disaster scenarios at the exact same time, trying to sit at a pub and make small talk about the football game or someone's new car... it just feels impossible. It’s like trying to have a casual chat while you're watching a building burn down. You just can't do it. So no, it's not their opinions I'm worried about. I'm just too exhausted and wound up by everything else going wrong to even try to maintain a social life right now.
Do you feel like your worrying and the situations it puts you in are changing how you see yourself as a person?

Changing how I see myself? I mean... no. Not really. I don't think I'm having some kind of, you know, existential identity crisis over all this. I know exactly who I am. I'm still the same guy who spent the last twenty years managing IT infrastructures. I don't look in the mirror and see a stranger or think my core values have shifted or anything like that. 

It's not a fundamental change in my personality. I mean, I still want to be the guy who fixes things, the guy who keeps the systems running smoothly, which is what I always was. It's just that right now... well, it's like I'm the exact same machine, built with the exact same hardware, but my operating system is completely corrupted. Like, the specs on paper are identical to what they were five years ago, but if you try to run even the most basic executable file—like sending an email or just sitting quietly—the whole thing just freezes and crashes. 

So I don't see myself as a *different* person. I just see myself as a profoundly broken version of the person I've always been. I know I'm still me. I'm just a me that has absolutely zero processing power left to give. Does that make sense? It's not that my self-image has changed into something else, it's just... I'm incredibly frustrated with my current operating state. I'm just so angry that I can't function the way I know I'm supposed to, the way I used to when I could actually handle the pressure of an outage without falling apart. So, no, my identity is completely intact, for whatever that's worth. It's just buried under all this constant, exhausting noise.
